Q: Git pull / push - unable to access HTTPS, SSL routines seem to be down A:

Received a similar error recently stderr: fatal: unable to access 'https://github.com/org/repo/': TLS connect error: error:0A000419:SSL routines::tlsv1 alert access denied

In addition to the existing answers, I wanted to mention that as of 2026/03/02, while there could be an issue with the version of TLS used, tlsv1 in this warning seems to be a generic label used by OpenSSL for access denied exceptions. It's listed in crypto/err/openssl.txt as SSL_R_TLSV1_ALERT_ACCESS_DENIED:1049:tlsv1 alert access denied.

So I think that any instance where the server is denying access to your client could trigger this. In my case, the culprit was anti-virus was blocking https://www.github.com. Git and OpenSSL shouldn't be trying to use TLSv1 by default so don't be like me and focus too much on the tlsv1 bit if your setup seems correct.

Q: Replace values in a CSV string A:

Assuming SQL Server 2005 or better, and assuming order isn't important, then given this split function:

CREATE FUNCTION [dbo].[SplitInts]
(
   @List       VARCHAR(MAX),
   @Delimiter  CHAR(1)
)
RETURNS TABLE
AS
   RETURN ( SELECT Item FROM ( SELECT Item = x.i.value('(./text())[1]', 'int') 
    FROM 
    ( SELECT [XML] = CONVERT(XML, '<i>' + REPLACE(@List, @Delimiter, '</i><i>') 
              + '</i>').query('.') ) AS a CROSS APPLY [XML].nodes('i') AS x(i)
          ) AS y WHERE Item IS NOT NULL);
GO

You can get this result in the following way:

;WITH x AS
(
    SELECT id, item, oldid, [newid], rn = ROW_NUMBER() OVER
    (PARTITION BY id 
     ORDER BY PATINDEX('%,' + RTRIM(s.Item) + ',%', ',' + t.plist + ','))
    FROM #tmp AS t CROSS APPLY dbo.SplitInts(t.plist, ',') AS s
    LEFT OUTER JOIN #tmpprod AS p ON p.oldid = s.Item
)
SELECT id, newlist = STUFF((SELECT ',' + RTRIM(COALESCE([newid], Item)) 
    FROM x AS x2 WHERE x2.id = x.id
    FOR XML PATH(''), 
    TYPE).value(N'./text()[1]', N'varchar(max)'), 1, 1, '') 
FROM x GROUP BY id;

Results:

id newlist
1 111,11,112,17,113
2 22,222,333,25
3 109,6,8,110

Note that the ROW_NUMBER() / OVER / PARTITION BY / ORDER BY is only there to try to coerce the optimizer to return the rows in that order. You may observe this behavior today and it can change tomorrow depending on statistics or data changes, optimizer changes (service packs, CUs, upgrade, etc.) or other variables.

Long story short: if you're depending on that order, just send the set back to the client, and have the client construct the comma-delimited list. It's probably where this functionality belongs anyway.

That said, in SQL Server 2017+, we can guarantee retaining the order by splitting with OPENJSON() and reassembling with STRING_AGG():

;WITH x AS 
(
  SELECT o.id, val = COALESCE(n.newid, p.value), p.[key] 
  FROM #tmp AS o CROSS APPLY 
    OPENJSON('["' + REPLACE(o.pList, ',', '","') + '"]') AS p
  LEFT OUTER JOIN #tmpprod AS n 
  ON p.value = n.oldid
)
SELECT id, newlist = STRING_AGG(val, ',')
  WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY CONVERT(int, [key]))
  FROM x GROUP BY id;

Q: Remove specific strings from comma separated string values A:

Martin's answer is perfect if you don't need an explicit guarantee that the string will get reassembled in the same order as it arrived (while you should generally observe that to be the case, that's no guarantee). If you do need that guarantee, then on SQL Server 2022+ (or Azure SQL Database/MI), you can use the new enable_ordinal argument of STRING_SPLIT:

SELECT @BaseStringValues = STRING_AGG(value, ',') 
                           WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ordinal)
  FROM
  (
    SELECT value, ordinal
      FROM STRING_SPLIT(@BaseStringValues, ',', 1) -- order matters
  ) AS x
  WHERE NOT EXISTS
  (
    SELECT 1 
      FROM STRING_SPLIT(@ParamValues, ',', 0) -- order doesn't matter
      WHERE value = x.value
  );

If you are on SQL Server 2017 or better, you can use OPENJSON, being careful to note that [key] is actually a string, so you need to treat it as a number (thanks T N):

SET @BaseStringValues = '["' + REPLACE(
  STRING_ESCAPE(@BaseStringValues, 'json'), ',','","') + '"]';

SELECT @BaseStringValues = STRING_AGG(value, ',')
                           WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY CONVERT(int, [key]))
  FROM OPENJSON(@BaseStringValues) AS x
  WHERE NOT EXISTS 
  (
    SELECT 1 FROM STRING_SPLIT(@ParamValues, ',')
    WHERE value = x.value
  );

If you are on SQL Server 2016 or lower, you are running an unsupported version and will have to resort to really ugly FOR XML PATH aggregation, which I talked about here, and an order-observing table-valued function to perform the split, which I talked about here.

Q: Why do we need the “finally:” clause in Python, if we can just write code after the “try:” block? A:

Here you can see how try, except, else, and finally work together. Actually, since your code doesn't have 'else' then what you claimed is right. I.e., There is no difference between the two statements that you wrote. But if 'else' is used somewhere, then 'finally' makes a difference

Q: What's your favorite Git command in 2026? A:

I wouldn't call it my "favorite", but I regularly use two specific features of rebase that are nice time savers:

  1. We have some repos that use the gitworkflow branching strategy. We reset the next branch every 2 weeks, and after we do, in-flight branches that may have come from next need to be rewritten for the new base. So, git rebase [previous-next-commit] my-feature-branch --onto origin/next does the trick in one command.
  2. Lately I've been using git commit --fixup=<commit-id> quite regularly and then later git rebase -i --autosquash. I especially use this often when coding with AI. (Currently) I like to commit the AI work as is, and then fix it up after the fact with new easily squashable commits so I can assess how much I have to tweak it.

Q: Want to build & install Glibc in Android (bionic) A:

I don't want to offend you, but you are essentially wasting your time trying to compile glibc with bionic compilers. To compile glibc, you need glibc (i.e. glibc-based compiler and dependencies) - this is the most correct approach. It may be possible to compile glibc with bionic, but the setup process will be terribly complicated and time consuming (plus, it will be a completely different library, in effect).

Also, I want to say that you configured PREFIX incorrectly in configure. It's better to separate glibc and all its bases from the bionic-based termux system, then you risk breaking termux. In addition to properly configuring configure, one should remove running unsupported system calls in glibc source files, this is important as such system calls can cause a Bad system call error when starting any glibc-based program.

For understanding, I have experience compiling glibc for termux - https://github.com/Maxython/glibc-for-termux.

Q: Google Sheets ARRAY_ROW issue with sorting a pass-through LAMBDA. Additional empty rows cause formula to error A:

your ARRAY_ROW issue is fundamentally same as any other ARRAY_ROW or ARRAY_LITERAL error. it arises from a dimensional mismatch of the individual components within the virtual array { } construct, regardless if it is standalone or within LAMBDA/QUERY or any other formula.

based on the insufficient/non-reproducible dataset in your question, there are maximum of only two spots in your formula that can produce this ARRAY_ROW error and with usage of new formulae, everything can be now fully avoided.

=SORT(LET(s, " where A starts with 'X'", 
          a, 'Alias Key Raw'!A:B,
          r, 'Designation Date Raw'!A2:A, 
          d, XLOOKUP(TOCOL(G2:G, 1), TOCOL(r, 1), TOCOL(OFFSET(r,,1), 1)),
          k, QUERY(a, "select A"&s, ), 
          v, SPLIT(REGEXREPLACE(QUERY(a, "select B"&s, ), "\*", ""), ","),
 HSTACK(d, k, v)), 1, 0, 2, 0)

using HSTACK will never produce ARRAY_ERROR of any kind and all other possible errors are passed from down the line to the HSTACK
